# When Prison Art Gets Political

**Channel:** the-canvas
**URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v6Z8S8A41qI
**Views:** est. 500K views
**Language:** English (en)
**Auto-generated:** False

---

Art made from prison, or from having experienced 
imprisonment, can be some of the most important  
works of art made as they show, not only the 
living conditions of prisoners which are too  
often hidden from the public, but also the 
political conditions inherent to incarceration.
In this video, we’ll look at three different 
artworks by three different artists who were  
all imprisoned for their political beliefs 
or actions and who made artworks either  
during or after their imprisonment. 
What can we learn by looking at these  
artworks? What do they tell us about 
dissent, repression and the State?
The first prisoner we’ll be looking 
at is Gustave Courbet’s self-portrait:  
Self-Portrait at Sainte-Pelagie, made in 1872.
Gustave Courbet was an incredibly controversial 
painter at the time, and he painted this artwork  
at the peak of his career. He had made several 
self-portraits during his career, many successful  
ones, including this one as a Desperate Man 
which is probably his most famous. However,  
in self-portrait at Sainte-Pelagie, Courbet isn’t 
as confrontational. He’s sitting pensively by a  
window, almost expressionless. He’s looking out 
of a window which contrasts the shadowy interior  
he’s confined in with the sunny exterior he’s cast 
out of. If you pay enough attention, you’ll notice  
that this window has iron bars obstructing 
it. Gustave Courbet is sitting in jail.
And he left us a clue as to why he’s 
sitting in jail. He’s wearing a red scarf,  
symbolic of the Paris Commune which happened 
only a year before this self-portrait was made.
Gustave Courbet was pretty radical, especially 
for his time. He was friends with Pierre-Joseph  
Proudhon, a socialist theorist 
who was the first person to call  
themselves an anarchist. He’d even paint 
a portrait of the man with his children.
As an example of his radicalness, 
just 6 months before the Commune,  
he said that the Colonne Vendôme, am imperialist 
monument, should be dissembled and relocated: 
 “In as much as the Vendôme Column is a 
monument devoid of all artistic value,  
tending to perpetuate by its expression the ideas 
of war and conquest of the past imperial dynasty,  
which are reproved by a republican nation’s 
sentiment, citizen Courbet expresses the wish  
that the National Defence government will 
authorize him to disassemble this column.”
This wasn’t necessarily a new idea as even Marx 
used the image of the toppling of this monument  
in 1852 in the conclusion to his pamphlet 
The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte:  
“But when the imperial mantle finally 
falls on the shoulders of Louis Bonaparte,  
the bronze statue of Napoleon will come crashing 
down from the top of the Vendôme Column.”
So Courbet, through his associations and perhaps 
propositions, was a controversial figure,  
and we didn’t talk about his controversial 
artworks. L’Origine du monde, for example,  
made in 1866, gave me a strike on my channel. The 
video about it is still up however. I’m censoring  
the painting here, but it’s not censored 
in the video about it. Go check it out.
Courbet went from a figure of controversy to 
an insurrectionary figure in 1871 when the  
Paris Commune started. The Paris Commune was an 
insurrection rallying socialists, communists and  
anarchists behind an anti-authoritarian project 
for the city of Paris which was under siege by  
the Prussian army. Paris was self-managed by 
the working class and Courbet was among them:
“Paris is a true paradise!
No police, no nonsense,  
no exaction of any kind, no arguments! 
If only it could stay like this forever…
it is a beautiful dream.”
So during this beautiful dream, 
this insurrectionary project,  
which I strongly encourage you to read more about, 
Courbet was elected to the Commune’s council. He  
was also the president of the Artist Federation, 
promoting the ideas that artists should be in  
charge of art instead of the government or 
the Salon. However, things turned a bit sour.
The Colonne Vendôme ended up being toppled, the 
French army took over Paris after 72 days of the  
Commune, and between 10 and 20 thousand communards 
were murdered in a period called the ‘Bloody  
Week’. Courbet survived, but was nonetheless 
captured, imprisoned and told to personally pay  
for the restoration of the Vendome column, a cost 
of over 300,000 francs which he could never repay.  
He was bankrupt, exiled himself to Switzerland 
from 1873 until his death in 1877. This is the  
only artwork he ever made about the commune, 
this red scarf being the only allusion to it.
Over a century later, in 2011, in China,  
an artist was arrested and put in prison 
for 81 days without trial for tax evasion.  
However, especially because this artist 
is known for his criticism of the Chinese  
government and his human rights activism, it’s 
widely believed that these charges were simply  
an excuse to intimidate him. This artist, also 
controversial, is the very notorious: Ai Weiwei.
Following his imprisonment, Ai made an 
installation presenting 6 scenes: Supper,  
Accusers, Cleansing, Ritual, Entropy, and 
Doubt. The installation is titled SACRED.
These scenes are contained in 6,5ft x 12ft iron 
boxes which you can only see the content of,  
through small openings. In a voyeuristic 
way, you see scenes from Ai’s detention  
which not only show the oppressive and 
suffocating environment in which he lived,  
but also the constant surveillance he 
was under. This constant surveillance,  
of course shown through the presence of prison 
guards, is heightened by our own presence as a  
viewer. Looking at Ai’s work is to surveil him, 
it’s to voyeuristically watch and do nothing.
Perhaps the enclosed boxes are meant to 
convey a sense of confinement, a feeling  
that Ai is truly trapped in there. But the way 
I interpret the way this artwork is experienced  
is by turning the viewers’ gaze into a tool of 
oppression, to turn our participation into the  
surveillance criticized in the artwork. If the 
State is oppressing Ai, and if the State gains  
legitimacy through both our action and inaction, 
then we are legitimizing Ai’s suppression.
If Courbet made a self-portrait in 
prison dejectedly sitting by a window,  
Ai makes several self-portraits interacting 
with guards and frontally showing his living  
conditions. He’s also confronting the viewers 
with their own role regarding his situation  
through their inaction facing repressive 
governments around the world. In this sense,  
though both artworks depict imprisonment, 
both have very different aims. One feels  
like a testimony of an experience, the other is 
a denouncement of it and a call to change it.
But Shawn, I’m not from China or Russia, 
I’m from a free country! I’m from the UK!  
Ai Weiwei can’t seriously tell me that 
I’m ok with putting activists in prison.
When I visited the UK, I went 
to Hastings to meet Sue Tilley,  
friend of Leigh Bowery and model of Lucian 
Freud which I interviewed in this video,  
and I decided to visit Hastings 
Contemporary, a museum which  
featured an exhibition by Isabel Rock. Rock’s 
installation was the highlight of my visit.
“Welcome to your cell, come on in, 
take a seat, make yourself at home,  
please sit on the bed or the 
chair, don’t mind your roommate.”
At Hasting’s contemporary, you could walk 
into an exact replica of the prison cell  
Isabel Rock spent a month in, following a Just 
Stop Oil action where she climbed on gantries  
on a highway in the UK in 2022. She was later 
found not guilty after a jury deemed, after  
only an hour of deliberation, that her climate 
action was motivated by a ‘reasonable excuse’.
In the perfect replica of the cell, 
which is in itself an artwork,  
you could find artworks made by Rock from 
her cell during her imprisonment, which,  
in an interview you can watch on the channel 
Art Plugged on Youtube, she explains she drew  
to help with her mental health. In that same 
interview, she describes her stay in prison,  
how it affected her and why she doesn’t 
regret it. I recommend watching it.
I loved Isabel Rock’s installation and it was, 
even more-so than Tracey Emin’s exhibition at  
Tate, my favourite artwork I experienced on my 
trip in the UK. It put you right in the middle  
of it, not as a voyeur, but as a participant. It’s 
putting you in the shoes of a political prisoner.  
It’s telling you it could happen to you. Not 
only did it underline the increasingly repressive  
measures the State is enacting to quell political 
action, it was also a personal testimony of that  
repression, it’s confirming that this kind of 
coercion isn’t only present in the past, as shown  
by Courbet, or in overtly authoritarian countries 
as shown by Ai, but also in liberal democracies.
What these artworks make evident is that, no 
matter where there is authority, hierarchy,  
or any concentration of power, there will 
be resistance to it. That resistance will  
always be dealt with suppression, with state 
violence. And to anarchists such as myself,  
this is inevitable in any hierarchical 
society. As long as you have people in power,  
there will be people who won’t like it, people 
who feel like it’s unfair that someone has more  
power than them. No matter what, and it 
way not come immediately or successfully,  
there will always be dissent and resistance; 
it may not articulate itself ideologically  
as anarchism, it might not even 
be directly intellectualized,  
but it is present everywhere because freedom, 
far than being just an abstract value,  
is a human instinct. And it is one that we see 
on display when artists make art about prisons.
